questions: Can you move my domain over?
Yes. Type in the domain you already have. With supported domain companies it connects in one click, and email can come from it too.

Yes. You can take card payment when someone books, so a no-show doesn't cost you the slot.

Yes. AnyPress works with HighLevel, so the people who book or write in can land in your HighLevel contacts too.

problems.body: You may be the best in town, but if no one knows it, you don't get the business.

problems.title: Customer details live on scraps of paper
problems.body: Names and numbers are in your phone, your truck and a notebook, so nobody hears from you again.

problems.title: Your community lives elsewhere
problems.body: Lessons in one app, discussions in another, payments in a third, and none of it on your domain.

problems.body: Many charge a monthly fee and a slice of every course you sell, or a price per student.

problems.title: Your students belong to the platform

problems.title: Dues by spreadsheet
problems.body: Renewals, reminders and who has paid are tracked by hand, every year.

problems.title: Events in another app
problems.body: Tickets and sign-ups live somewhere different from your website, with another bill.

problems.title: Members have nowhere to meet
problems.body: News goes out by email blast and the members' directory is a PDF that's out of date.

problems.title: Giving through a separate app
problems.body: Online giving lives in one tool, with its own fees, and the website somewhere else.

problems.title: Sign-ups on paper and in group chats
problems.body: Events and volunteer rotas are spread over sheets, texts and chats that newcomers never see.

problems.title: One volunteer knows how it works
problems.body: The site was set up by someone who has moved on, and now no one wants to touch it.

problems.title: Every location does its own thing
problems.body: Different builders, different looks and different logins make the brand hard to keep consistent.

problems.title: Every change goes through head office
problems.body: When one central site holds every location, a new opening time or local offer waits in someone's inbox.

problems.title: Each new location adds a full bill
problems.body: Every location pays full price for its own website, so growing costs the same per site forever.

can.title: Your website too
items: As many pages as you need, and a blog
Ready-made page layouts to start from
Titles, previews and a sitemap set up for Google
Redirects and a log of broken links
Your own domain and emails from your own address
Bring your current WordPress site with a free plugin

problem: A different tool for every job
A shop, a booking tool, a course platform and a help desk that don't talk to each other.
fix: One site does it all
Shop, bookings, members' area and courses together, with one record for every customer.

problem: Customer questions get lost
Emails about orders and bookings pile up in your inbox with no way to track them.
fix: A help desk built in
Questions become tickets you and your team can answer and track, on your own site.

problem: Growing means moving
Outgrow a simple site and you rebuild somewhere else.
fix: Room to grow
Switch on parts as you need them and move up a size any time. Your site stays where it is.

questions: Why not buy two smaller plans?
Everything puts all the tools on one site, so a customer who buys, books and joins is one person, not three. It also costs less than the four other plans together, and adds a help desk.
Do I have to use every part?
No. Switch on what you need today. The rest is ready when you are.
Which size should I pick?
Small suits most new sites. Busy shops and big communities usually move to Medium or Large, and you can change any time.
Is it harder to look after?
No. We apply security fixes to every part and save it every night, the same as any other AnyPress site.

GUIDES.title: Moving your shop: a step-by-step checklist
GUIDES.lead: How to move an online shop to a new home without losing sales, customers or your place on Google.

sections.heading: Before you start
checks: Export your products (names, prices, descriptions, photos) from your current shop
Export your customer list, and note who agreed to get emails
Write down every page address that gets visits, so none of them break
List your active subscriptions and when they renew
Pick a quiet week. Avoid a sale or a launch

sections.heading: Build the new shop next to the old one
steps: Start your new shop on its free address. Your old shop keeps running.
Add your products and photos, then check prices, shipping and taxes.
Connect your payment account and place a test order.
Copy your About, Contact, Shipping and Refund pages.
Import your customer list with each person's email consent as it was.

sections.heading: Switch over
steps: Point your domain at the new shop. Visitors arrive there from that moment.
Send old page addresses to their new pages, so links and Google results keep working.
Tell your customers by email, and update the link in your social profiles.
Keep the old shop open (not selling) for a month in case you need anything from it.

sections.heading: Subscriptions
sections.body: Existing subscribers usually have to sign up again on the new shop, because card details can't be copied from one payment setup to another. Give them a simple link and a reason to do it, like a first month at a lower price.

GUIDES.title: Local trades website checklist
GUIDES.lead: What a plumber, electrician or any local trade needs on a website to get found nearby and get booked.

sections.heading: Get found nearby
checks: Your business name, phone number and the towns you cover on every page
A page for each service you want more of, in the words customers search for
A free Google Business Profile that links to your website
A few photos of real jobs, with a line on what you did and where

sections.heading: Make it easy to book
steps: Put a Book a time button at the top of every page.
List the jobs people can book online and how long each takes.
Take a deposit for longer jobs, so a no-show doesn't cost you the slot.
Turn on reminder emails the day before.

sections.heading: Look like a real business
checks: Email from your own domain, not a free address
Your licence and insurance details where customers can see them
Clear prices or a starting price for common jobs

sections.heading: Keep customers coming back
sections.body: Every booking adds the customer to your list. A short email after the job, and a seasonal reminder (like a furnace check before winter), brings repeat work without a single phone call.

GUIDES.title: Regulated store checklist
GUIDES.lead: What to have in place before you sell supplements, CBD or other regulated products from your own store.

sections.heading: Payments
checks: A payment account that has approved your products in writing
A backup payment option in case your main one pauses your account
Clear refund and cancellation terms that match what your payment provider expects

sections.heading: On every product page
checks: The label and ingredient information, as on the packaging
Any warnings your products legally need
No health claims you can't support
Age checks where the law asks for them

sections.heading: Pages your store needs
checks: Terms, Privacy, Refund and Shipping pages
A contact page with a real email address
Where you ship, and where you don't

sections.heading: Good to know
sections.body: Rules depend on what you sell and where. This checklist is a starting point, not legal advice. Check the rules for your products with someone who knows them.

sections.heading: What to look for on your current bill
checks: The monthly or yearly plan price
A percentage taken from each sale
Extra charges per student, per course or per admin
Add-ons you pay for separately (email, community, payments)

GUIDES.title: Member website program: a one-page guide
GUIDES.lead: How a chamber or association can offer members their own websites, as a benefit or as a new source of income.

sections.heading: How it works
steps: You apply as a seller and get your own shop, under your organisation's name.
You pick which kinds of sites to offer members, and set your prices.
Members buy from your shop. We build and look after each site.
You pay per site, and the price per site drops at 3, 10 and 25 sites.

sections.heading: Two ways to run it
checks: As a member benefit: price sites at cost, and point to it when members renew
As income: add a monthly margin on each site to fund your programs

sections.heading: Your first month
steps: Pick three members who need a website and offer them a first-month discount.
Mention it in your newsletter and at your next event.
Ask those first members if you can show their sites to others.

What to expect on a first visit, including parking and children's programs
A way to ask a question or a prayer request

sections.heading: For members

Events and volunteer sign-ups
Sermons or livestream links
A weekly email with what's coming up

sections.heading: For your team

Nobody has to look after the website itself

GUIDES.title: Rolling out 10 locations: a worked example
GUIDES.lead: How a brand with ten locations can give each one its own site from one starting point, and what it costs.

sections.heading: The plan
steps: Head office applies as a seller and builds one site the way every location should look.
Each location gets a copy, with its own address, hours, staff and bookings.
Locations update their own details. Head office keeps the look and the offers the same.

sections.heading: What it costs
sections.body: Ten Bookings sites at $19 each is $190 a month at full price. At ten sites the volume discount is 20%, so it comes to $152 a month for all ten.

sections.heading: Who pays
checks: Head office pays for every site and charges locations through the franchise fee, or
Each location buys its own site from head office's shop

GUIDES.title: Your first site from the API, step by step
GUIDES.lead: Create a WordPress site for one of your customers from your own code.

sections.heading: Steps
steps: Ask us for API access from the contact page. You'll get a key and a secret.
Create a site with one call to /v1/tenants, giving it a name and your customer's email address.
Wait for the tenant.ready webhook, or check the site's status.
Send your customer their sign-in link. They open WordPress with one click.

sections.heading: Where to read more
sections.body: The API reference, the TypeScript and PHP SDKs and example code are in the public API repository, linked from the developers page.
